extracted.intended_audience: literary scholars, critics, editors, and educated readers of Coleridge/romantic poetry
extracted.subtask_description: Evaluative guidance for judging/producing literary works (poetry and prose), focusing on originality, arrangement, exposition, attribution, and reader accessibility as discussed in a scholarly introduction to Coleridge. Useful for critics, editors, and literary biographers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Originality / claim to fundamental ideas
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims to having 'anticipated' or possessed the 'main and fundamental ideas' of another thinker must be treated with caution; the writer's allegation that 'the principal points of Schelling's system were not new to him' is a central issue.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate originality by checking concrete tests (dates, publication history, explicit acknowledgements). Accept that genuine coincidences or independent discovery are possible — especially where multiple minds work in the same intellectual climate — but avoid asserting originality without supporting evidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Acknowledgement and use of sources (quotation/translation attribution)
rubrics_metrics.description: Unacknowledged use of another's words or partial translations (e.g., passages 'in part translated' from other writers) has been used as a pretext for accusations of plagiarism.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Authors and editors should clearly state borrowings and translations when republishing; omission can indicate carelessness or disregard for reputation rather than deliberate dishonesty, but proper citation avoids dispute. When evaluating a work, note whether editors added or removed references and whether the author supervised the edition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Arrangement and methodising of thought
rubrics_metrics.description: The 'skill in arranging and methodizing of thought with a view to publication' is crucial; a 'want of proportion in the faculties' or inability to adapt thought to the capacities of a volume prevents producing many or good books.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether the material is organized into a coherent plan appropriate to its form (essay, book, lecture). Beware of works that abandon a stated plan and become miscellaneous; evaluate whether the arrangement helps the reader grasp the argument and whether the writer has the craft to shape deep thought into publishable form.

rubrics_metrics.name: Illustration and vivid exposition (use of examples)
rubrics_metrics.description: The 'want of illustrative examples and vivid exposition' is identified as 'the main defect' in some prose, sometimes occasioned by a 'dread of being tedious.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether the author supplies sufficient examples and exposition to render abstract ideas intelligible. If omission stems from wanting to avoid tedium, weigh the trade-off: too few illustrations make writing unintelligible; too many may bore. Good exposition balances clarity and concision.

rubrics_metrics.name: Clarity and intelligibility relative to intended reader
rubrics_metrics.description: Critics may call certain prose 'unintelligible'; such works often aim 'to make the reader to think' rather than to provide instant lucidity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Judge clarity against the intended reader's preparation and purpose. Writing that deliberately demands intellectual effort can be legitimate, but its success depends on whether readers are given adequate scaffolding (exposition, examples) to follow the thought.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reader effort required / accessibility of new thought
rubrics_metrics.description: ‘The minds that are to receive these accessions must themselves... be renewed proportionately’ — new thought requires that readers undertake a process of mental renewal and struggle.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When assessing innovation, account for the degree of reader work required. Writers introducing novel ideas should anticipate that readers need time and internal cooperation; consider whether the text supports that process or simply expects it without facilitation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Balance between speculative depth and literary execution
rubrics_metrics.description: A writer's 'marvellous intellectual gifts' can be undermined by 'intellectual impairments' — a lack of proportion between speculative ambition and the practical literary skill to present it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate whether the craft (structure, phrasing, selection) matches the ambition of the ideas. Deep speculation is valuable, but without corresponding execution (editing, arrangement, method), the work may fail to communicate effectively.

rubrics_metrics.name: Editorial supervision and prudence in editions
rubrics_metrics.description: If an author 'had superintended the edition' he might have made proper references; editors sometimes add material (e.g., verses from Schiller or Stolberg) that should be attributed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess the edition's fidelity to authorial intent and the transparency of editorial additions. Editors should identify insertions and sources; authors should, when possible, supervise editions to prevent misattribution or loss of context.

rubrics_metrics.name: Metre, language, and translational fidelity in poetry
rubrics_metrics.description: Comparisons of metre and language (e.g., the English pentameter's dactylic flow versus the original) are used to judge poetic translation and adaptation — reproduction 'with additions and improvements' may be made acceptable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating poetic translations or adaptations, consider metrical flow, linguistic suitability, and whether the translator adds improvements or merely reproduces form. Assess both fidelity and the aesthetic success of rendered lines; improvements may be legitimate if acknowledged or clearly transformative.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tone and purpose: awakening reflection versus seeking popularity
rubrics_metrics.description: Some writers 'loved to go forward expanding and ennobling the soul' and 'had no hope of gainful popularity' — their purpose was to awaken reflection rather than to chase ephemeral applause.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Determine the authorial aim: if the work intends to provoke deep reflection, judge it by its ability to do so rather than by mass appeal. Conversely, if the intended goal is popularity or immediate effect, assess clarity, ornament, and readability accordingly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evidence and tests for priority versus coincidence
rubrics_metrics.description: Accusations of borrowing or priority ought to be tested by concrete means (dates, publications); the text notes that 'to say... he had come to the end of all that Schelling had taught... is a perfectly false light' absent such tests.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating claims of priority, seek documentary evidence (manuscripts, dated notes, earlier publications). Consider the intellectual milieu — similar discoveries may arise independently — and avoid condemning similarity without chronological support.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoidance of vanity and cautious self-presentation
rubrics_metrics.description: The author sometimes defended himself from charges of 'neglecting to employ... his natural gifts' and was 'goaded into some degree of egotism by the charges' — presentation of one's powers and claims affects reception.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess how the author's self-presentation (claims of originality, emphasis on genius) influences credibility. Excessive self-promotion invites scrutiny; modest but clear exposition of contributions with evidence is preferable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Maintain coherence: avoid filling work with miscellaneous desk-content
rubrics_metrics.description: The work 'abandons its plan' and the book is 'filled out to a certain size, with such miscellaneous contents as his desk presented' — resulting in lack of method and abrupt termination.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate whether material is relevant to the stated plan. A coherent, planned structure is preferable to a miscellany. If miscellany exists, judge it on the internal quality of items and whether editorial framing explains inclusions.
